title: Concurrency Hazards — Livelock & Starvation
summary: The hazard family beyond simple races — livelock, starvation, and priority inversion, told through the real Mars Pathfinder incident.

slides.markdown:
Beyond [race conditions](race-conditions-and-critical-sections) and deadlock, concurrent systems fail in two more distinctive ways: **livelock** (threads stay busy but make no real progress) and **starvation** (one thread is repeatedly denied a resource it needs). This topic also covers **priority inversion**, a specific starvation mechanism famous for nearly ending a NASA mission.

Deadlock gets its own full topic elsewhere in this group's curriculum; here the focus is on telling these four hazards apart cleanly, since interviewers frequently probe exactly that distinction to check you're not using "race condition" as a catch-all word for every concurrency bug.

slides.sectionTitle: The concurrency hazard family: race, deadlock, livelock, starvation
slides.markdown:
Four distinct failure modes get lumped together colloquially, but each has a precise meaning worth keeping straight. A **race condition** is a correctness bug where the outcome depends on timing. A **deadlock** is a set of threads each waiting on a resource held by another in the set, forming a cycle — nobody can proceed, and nobody is even trying (they're all blocked). A **livelock** is threads that are *not* blocked — they're actively running — but their actions keep undoing each other's progress. **Starvation** is one specific thread being perpetually denied a resource while others repeatedly get it, even though the system as a whole keeps making progress.

The throughline: deadlock and livelock are both about zero forward progress for the threads involved, while starvation is about *unfair* progress — the system moves forward, just never for this one thread.

slides.sectionTitle: Livelock: busy but making no progress
slides.markdown:
A classic livelock example: two threads each hold a resource and, on detecting they can't get the other's resource, politely release their own and retry — and if their retry timing stays synchronized, they can do this forever, each releasing just as the other tries to grab it. Both threads are constantly active, using CPU, executing real instructions — nothing is blocked — yet neither ever completes its task.

This is distinct from a busy-wait spinlock (which is *intended* to loop until progress is possible) — livelock is an *unintended* loop where the retry logic itself, meant to be a polite deadlock-avoidance mechanism, is what causes the failure. It commonly shows up in retry-and-backoff logic that isn't randomized: two processes retrying at exactly the same fixed interval can stay perfectly out of sync with success indefinitely.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: two threads politely "after you" — livelock illustrated
slides.markdown:
![Livelock hallway example](assets/livelock-hallway.svg)

The visual point is that both people are clearly moving the whole time — nothing about the picture looks "stuck" the way a deadlock would (frozen, waiting) — which is exactly why livelock can be harder to notice at a glance: CPU and thread activity graphs look busy and healthy while zero real work gets done.

slides.sectionTitle: Starvation: always losing the race for a resource
slides.markdown:
**Starvation** is when a specific thread is repeatedly denied a resource it needs, even though the system overall keeps functioning and other threads keep getting served. It doesn't require anything as dramatic as a deadlock or livelock — just a scheduling or fairness policy that happens to always favor someone else.

A concrete cause: a naive scheduler that always picks the highest-priority ready thread will starve any lower-priority thread for as long as higher-priority work keeps arriving — the low-priority thread is never technically blocked forever, it's just never chosen. This connects directly back to the [readers-writers problem](classic-synchronization-problems): the readers-priority solution starves writers exactly this way, by always favoring readers whenever any are active.

slides.sectionTitle: Priority inversion: a low-priority task blocking a high-priority one
slides.markdown:
**Priority inversion** is a specific, sneaky mechanism that causes starvation: a low-priority thread acquires a lock, then a high-priority thread needs that same lock and blocks waiting for it — so far, expected. The dangerous part is when a **medium-priority** thread (that needs neither the lock nor anything from the high-priority thread) is ready to run and preempts the low-priority thread, since the scheduler sees it as higher priority than the lock holder. Now the medium-priority thread runs freely while the high-priority thread waits — effectively, the low-priority thread's lock has inverted the priority order, letting medium-priority work block high-priority work indirectly.

Without intervention this can continue as long as medium-priority work keeps arriving, since the low-priority lock-holder never gets scheduled to finish and release the lock — turning a small locking dependency into an unbounded, unpredictable delay for the highest-priority thread in the system.

slides.sectionTitle: The Mars Pathfinder priority-inversion story as a worked example
slides.markdown:
In 1997, NASA's **Mars Pathfinder** rover began experiencing unexplained total system resets days after landing. The cause, found by re-running the exact software on Earth: a low-priority thread managing a shared information bus held a mutex; a high-priority thread needing that bus would block waiting for it; and an unrelated medium-priority communications task would preempt the low-priority thread whenever it ran, keeping the mutex held far longer than intended. When the high-priority thread's watchdog timer, which expected the bus task to complete quickly, expired without the mutex being released, it assumed a fatal software fault and forced a full system reset — exactly the priority-inversion pattern from the previous slide, on a spacecraft 190 million kilometers away.

The fix, uploaded remotely after the bug was reproduced on an identical testbed on Earth: enable **priority inheritance** (next slide) on the mutex, which the VxWorks real-time OS supported but had been left disabled. This is one of the most cited real-world priority-inversion incidents precisely because it's a textbook case with a documented root cause, a working fix, and NASA-grade postmortem rigor — genuinely useful to cite by name in an interview.

**Priority inheritance** temporarily boosts a lock-holding thread's priority to match the highest priority of any thread currently waiting for that same lock. In the Pathfinder scenario, the moment the high-priority bus-management thread blocked on the mutex, the low-priority holder would be bumped to high priority for as long as it held the lock — meaning the medium-priority communications task could no longer preempt it, since it's no longer actually the lowest-priority runnable thread. The low-priority thread finishes quickly, releases the mutex, drops back to its normal priority, and the high-priority thread proceeds without ever waiting on the unrelated medium-priority work.

Most real-time operating systems and thread libraries support this as a mutex attribute (`PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT` in POSIX threads) rather than something you implement by hand — the interview-relevant point is recognizing *when* to enable it (any system mixing priorities with shared locks, especially real-time or embedded systems with hard deadlines) rather than implementing the mechanism yourself.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: race vs deadlock vs livelock vs starvation — telling them apart
slides.markdown:
| | Threads' state | Root cause | Fix direction |
|---|---|---|
| Race condition | Running normally | Missing synchronization on shared state | Add correct synchronization |
| Deadlock | Blocked, in a cycle | Circular resource acquisition | Break the cycle (ordering, timeouts, detection) |
| Livelock | Running, but futile | Retry/backoff logic that stays synchronized | Randomized backoff (jitter), breaking symmetry |
| Starvation | Sometimes running, never chosen for the resource | Unfair scheduling or lock policy | Fairness policy, priority inheritance, aging |

**Fast interview check:** ask "are the threads blocked, or are they running but getting nowhere?" — blocked-in-a-cycle is deadlock, running-but-futile is livelock, and "one specific thread never gets picked" (regardless of blocked or running) is starvation. Getting this triage right in the first ten seconds of an answer is what separates a candidate who's debugged real concurrency issues from one reciting definitions.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagnosing livelock and starvation in production
slides.markdown:
Both hazards are easy to miss with naive monitoring because CPU usage looks *healthy*, not idle — the opposite signature from lock contention (§ locks-and-mutexes), where blocked threads sleep and CPU looks under-used. The tell for **livelock** is high CPU or high retry-counter metrics with flat or zero completed-work throughput — if a service's "requests processed" graph is flat while its CPU graph is elevated, check for retry loops without randomized backoff between cooperating components (two services both backing off and retrying a lock or a distributed resource on the same fixed schedule is a common real cause).

The tell for **starvation** is a per-thread or per-request latency histogram with a long tail that never resolves — most requests complete fine, but a specific subset (often correlated with lower priority, arriving during high load, or a specific queue) never gets served, or gets served only after an unbounded wait. The fix is almost always adding explicit fairness: **aging** (gradually boosting a waiting thread's effective priority the longer it waits, so it eventually wins), a FIFO-fair lock instead of a naive one, or priority inheritance for the priority-inversion-specific case — the common thread is that none of these hazards get fixed by "just add more capacity," since the bug is about who gets picked, not how much total work the system can do.
